title: Maimonides' life
hookLine: born in Córdoba, he fled persecution and became a physician in Cairo

cards: A student wanted to visit a busy man in Egypt, and the man wrote back a warning: come if you like, but don't expect a long talk. Each morning he went to the palace as a doctor.

When he rode home, his hallway was already full: Jews and non-Jews, officials and ordinary people, all waiting to see him. He took one quick meal, then treated them until night. That picture comes from the letter itself.

The same man wrote a law code people still study and a philosophy book people still argue about. And he started out in Spain, in Córdoba, with a long road of flight between the two. Today, the life of the Rambam.

teach.b: Rambam is a name built from initials: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon. English speakers often call him Maimonides, son of Maimon. His father was a judge and scholar in Córdoba, and the boy grew up in that learned city.

teach.h: CONVERT OR LEAVE: THE FAMILY LEAVES.
teach.b: A new ruling movement, the Almohads, took power in Muslim Spain and North Africa and pressed Jews and Christians to convert or leave.

teach.h: FEZ, THE LAND OF ISRAEL, FUSTAT.
teach.b: The family chose the road: from place to place in Spain, across to Fez in Morocco, east to the land of Israel, and finally to Fustat, the old city of Cairo.
Picture it for a young scholar: books carried in bags, teachers left behind, no settled home for years. And yet he kept writing the whole way, a commentary on the Mishnah begun on the move.
In Egypt he became a physician, and in time a doctor to the court.
He led the Jewish community, answered legal questions in letters, and finished his great code of law, the Mishneh Torah, and later his philosophy book, the Guide for the Perplexed.
The Torah keeps reminding a people who had been strangers how to treat strangers.
In the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Rambam had been a stranger in many lands.
He ended up in Egypt itself, and his door was open to whoever came.

how: Jews around the world study the Rambam's Mishneh Torah, some following a daily study cycle, and his Thirteen Principles appear in prayer books in the form of the hymn Yigdal.

o: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, a refugee from Córdoba
the name of the code of law he wrote in Egypt
a Hebrew word for a doctor at a royal court

games.q: the Rambam's life — tap the pairs.

s: the Rambam spent his whole life in Spain
his family fled Córdoba, lived in Fez, sailed to the land of Israel and settled in Egypt.
in Egypt he became a doctor, in time to the court, and wrote of patients filling his hallway.
Maimonides and the Rambam are two different people
same man: Maimonides means son of Maimon; Rambam comes from the initials of his name.

games.q: you are a young scholar in Spain. a new ruler is pressing Jews to convert or leave. what does the Rambam's family do?
o: stay and wait for it to pass.
take the road, and keep moving until they find a place to settle.
give up study and go into hiding for good.
games.why: they left, moved through Spain, crossed to Fez, sailed to the land of Israel and settled in Fustat. he kept writing all the way.

practice: Bring to mind someone who had to leave a home, a grandparent, a coworker, a neighbor, or the Rambam's family on the road, and follow their route one place at a time.
What did they carry, what did they leave, and who opened a door for them? If you pray, you can hold them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Rambam. Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, also called Maimonides: a refugee from Córdoba who became a doctor, a teacher of law and a philosopher in Egypt. Today's word.
